The Geeetech Voice Recognition Module enables true voice recognition (not just sound detection)—it can recognize up to 15 distinct voice commands, organized into 3 groups of 5 each. Before operation, you must load (import) one specific group via serial command; only that group's commands will be recognized.
Analog Interface: 3.5 mm mono microphone jack + microphone pin interface
Serial Protocol: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit; default baud rate is 9600 bps, configurable (e.g., 2400, 4800, 19200, 38400)
Common Mode: Returns readable string responses (e.g. "START\n", "Finish one\n")
Compact Mode: Returns concise byte codes (e.g. 0xcc for success, 0xe0 for error)
Recognition Accuracy: Claimed up to 99% in ideal environments
Issue a command like 0xAA 0x11 to start recording group 1. Each of the five commands in that group must be recorded in sequence.
After recording, send a command (e.g. 0xAA 0x21) to import that group so the module can recognize its commands.
The module listens via microphone. When a recorded command is recognized, it sends a corresponding byte over serial (e.g., 0x11, 0x12, etc.), allowing your microcontroller to act accordingly.

4093 – An IC with Four Schmitt Trigger NAND Gates
The 4093 is a CMOS chip with four NAND gates with a Schmitt trigger. Because each gate has two inputs and has four gates inside, it’s often referred to as a Quad 2-Input NAND Schmitt Trigger.

A NAND gate with a Schmitt trigger works more or less like a normal NAND gate. With the exception that the threshold for when it switches from LOW to HIGH is different from when it switches from HIGH to LOW.

blocks.text: What is a NAND gate with Schmitt Trigger?
First of all, a NAND gate is a logic gate that works like an AND gate with a NOT gate on the output. Therefore it’s often called NOT-AND.
A NAND gate built from AND and NOT gates
This means that a NAND gate gives a LOW output only when all inputs are HIGH as shown in the truth table below.
Truth Table for the NAND gate
But this is a Schmitt trigger NAND gate. What does that mean?
This has to do with at what voltage the gate will interpret the input as a LOW or a HIGH input:

For example for a normal (non-Schmitt Trigger) gate that is powered from 5V, the gate might say that any voltage above 2.5V is HIGH, and any voltage below 2.5V is LOW. So if the input is at 2.5V and swinging a bit up and down (as these signals tend to do), then the output would be uncertain.
But for a Schmitt trigger gate, the threshold voltage is different based on if the input changes from LOW to HIGH or from HIGH to LOW.

For example, if the input is currently LOW, then a Schmitt trigger gate might require the input voltage to go above for 3.5V to switch to HIGH. But when it has switched to HIGH, dropping a bit below 3.5V doesn’t matter. Because in order to switch back to LOW, the Schmitt trigger gate requires the input to go down below for example 1.5V.

The 74LS221 (74221) is a dual non-retrigger able monostable multivibrator that provides two independent one-shot circuits in a single 16-pin package. Each channel accepts both negative-transition and positive-transition trigger inputs, enabling flexible triggering schemes for diverse digital designs. Schmitt-triggered B inputs and internal latching give the device excellent noise immunity and predictable triggering behaviour.

Pulse width is set by external timing components (Rext and Cext) and follows the approximate relationship tw ≈ 0.7·Rext·Cext, allowing pulse durations from tens of nanoseconds up to milliseconds depending on component values. Once a pulse is initiated the output remains independent of further A/B input transitions (non-retriggerable), while an overriding clear input (CLR) can terminate the pulse early when required. Timing stability is ensured across supply and temperature ranges by internal compensation.

The device offers TTL-compatible rise/fall times and totem-pole outputs, and is available in multiple packages (PDIP, SOIC, SSOP, CDIP, etc.), making it straightforward to integrate in through-hole and surface-mount assemblies. Common uses include reset generation, pulse stretching, debouncing, and timing control where a compact, reliable single-shot solution is needed.

Its chassis is robust yet ergonomic, with the clamp-jaw mechanism integrated near the top and buttons placed for ease of operation. The meter’s display is clearly visible, often employing a dual display layout (e.g., showing voltage together with frequency or current together with frequency), which helps users monitor multiple parameters simultaneously without switching modes. With its built-in flashlight or backlight, it remains usable even in low-light workspaces or tight panels.

Internally, it’s built to handle relatively demanding AC current loads (up to 600 A), and is equipped to manage measurement stability via True RMS, plus functions like peak or inrush detection, which are critical for catching transient currents or start-up surges. The device supports filters (e.g. low-pass filter) to reduce interference from high-frequency noise, helping to stabilize readings in harsh or noisy electrical environments. The materials and safety design give it a confidence-inducing feel: protection of inputs, safety category rating, and build quality that can survive job-site transport and usage.

On the usability side, the UT202BT is smart in its connectivity: the Bluetooth feature enables remote reading or logging, meaning users don’t always have to be right next to the meter to record data. Battery operation keeps it portable, while the jaw opening size, weight, and grip make it usable with one hand. Visual and audio indicators help alert the operator to over-ranges, live voltage presence (NCV), or when readings exceed preset limits. Overall, the UT202BT is built to bridge the gap between everyday clamp meter functionality and modern smart-tool convenience, suitable for electricians, technicians, field maintenance, and diagnostics tasks.

The UNI‑T UT25A is an AC circuit breaker finder and GFCI socket tester designed for rapid and reliable identification of circuit breakers in live electrical circuits. The system comprises a plug‑in transmitter and a handheld receiver: the transmitter injects a tracking signal into the circuit, while the receiver emits audible beeps and flashes LEDs when the signal is detected. Sensitivity is adjustable via a combined power/sensitivity knob on the receiver, allowing precise pinpointing of the target breaker by reducing signal range once proximity is established.

The UT25A’s receiver also features line‑tracking LEDs to confirm continuity, while the transmitter’s GFCI socket test function uses three LEDs to display correct wiring or specific fault conditions (e.g., open ground, reversed hot/neutral). Housed in compact, lightweight enclosures, both units are powered by a single 9 V battery (type 1604/6F22) and conform to UL 61010‑1 and CSA C22.2 No. 61010‑1 safety standards.

Operating on standard North American voltages (90 – 120 V, 50 – 60 Hz), the UT25A is suitable for electricians and maintenance personnel in residential and commercial settings, providing a fast, non‑invasive, and user‑friendly method to trace breakers and verify outlet wiring without circuit shutdown
